summary: Describes single-ended strategies for changing the long-term key of TCP-MD5, which commonly secures BGP sessions between routers. These allow mostly unsynchronized key changes between organizations. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Two companies share a password, and changing it normally needs both to switch at exactly the same moment. This describes tricks so one side can change first without breaking things.

questions: how to change tcp md5 keys
subtitle: How to change TCP-MD5 keys without stopping BGP sessions

tldr.problem: TCP-MD5 secures BGP sessions, but changing the long-term key requires both organizations to switch at exactly the same time, making updates difficult and risky.
tldr.mechanism: Receivers accept multiple keys at once (testing each one), and senders use a preferred key once it has been validated by the other side. A brief window allows both sides to operate with old and new keys simultaneously.
tldr.outcome: Key changes can proceed with less coordination, reducing operational friction while maintaining secure sessions.

today: RFC 4808 remains an Informational RFC providing guidance for operational key changes in TCP-MD5 secured sessions, particularly for BGP. It has not been obsoleted, though RFC 4107 and RFC 3562 provide related guidance on key management strategy.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
TCP-MD5 is specified in RFC 2385 and is most commonly used to authenticate BGP sessions between routers operated by different organizations. However, the protocol provides no mechanism for changing the authentication key, and RFC 2385 was not designed with key changes in mind. There is no Key ID field in the option, so even with a key management protocol, both sides would need to switch their key at exactly the same moment, or the connection breaks.

In practice, coordinating a simultaneous key change between different organizations is operationally difficult and error-prone. If the keys become out of sync, the session drops and repair attempts become difficult because the organizations can no longer communicate securely on that channel.
sections.plainLanguage: Two companies use a secret password to verify they are talking to each other. If they need to change the password, they normally have to do it at exactly the same moment. If they mess up the timing, their secure connection breaks and they cannot talk to fix the problem.

sections.title: The Heuristic Solution
sections.content:
RFC 4808 describes a heuristic that permits key changes despite this protocol limitation. The solution separates reception and transmission into two different algorithms.

For reception, a receiver maintains a list of valid keys, each with a timestamp. When a segment arrives, the receiver tries each key in turn until one validates the message (or discards it if no key works). For performance, the receiver should test the most-recently-used key first. The newest key that successfully validates a segment is marked as preferred.

For transmission, the sender delays using any new key for a considerable time (typically days), following a manually configured threshold that both parties agree to out of band. However, if a key has been used successfully to validate an incoming segment, the sender should use that preferred key for transmissions. This signals to the far end that the key change is safe.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides can try to understand messages that came with either the old or new password. Once one side realizes the other side is successfully using the new password, it switches to the new password too. This lets them change passwords without perfect timing.

sections.title: Single-Ended and Double-Ended Operations
sections.content:
A single-ended operation occurs when only one end of the connection has this algorithm implemented. The end with the capability provisions the new key with a start time far in the future (so it will not be used spontaneously), then notifies the other end out-of-band that a key change can commence. When the other end is upgraded, it will start using the new key immediately for transmission and drop all segments using the old key. As soon as the upgraded side tries to transmit with the new key, the original side will mark it as preferred and switch all its transmissions to the new key, including retransmissions of segments rejected because they used the old key.

The main risk in single-ended operations is a silent host: a router that has nothing to transmit and thus never signals which key is preferred. To handle this, an upgraded machine should occasionally try alternate keys on retransmitted segments and probe for new unused keys during silent periods. Alternatively, application-level keepalive messages (such as BGP keepalives) can ensure neither end is completely silent.

A double-ended operation is similar but both sides deploy the new key at about the same time. One side configures a trigger point where it is reasonably certain the other side has installed the new key, then both sides mark the new key as preferred and switch over.
sections.plainLanguage: If only one company has the smart algorithm, it provisionally loads the new password way in the future, tells the other company to upgrade, and then when the other side starts using it, the first side switches over. If both companies have the algorithm, they can switch at almost the same time.

sections.title: Key Monitoring and Cleanup
sections.content:
Implementations should track when a key was last successfully used for transmission or reception. This information is displayed via MIB objects or command-line tools so a network operations center can monitor key usage. When a new key has been used successfully for both transmission and reception for a reasonable amount of time (typically longer than twice the maximum segment lifetime), the old key can be safely deleted.

Multiple keys also create a potential for CPU denial-of-service attacks, since the receiver must try multiple keys. Therefore, keeping the overlap period (when multiple keys exist) reasonably short is recommended. Additionally, the Generalized TTL Security Mechanism (RFC 3682) can help defend against certain attacks. In practice, most of the time only one key exists; virtually all of the remaining time there are only two keys in existence.
sections.plainLanguage: The system should keep track of when each password was last used. Once the new password has been working for long enough, the old one can be thrown away. Having multiple passwords at once creates some security risks, so the overlap should not be too long.
